# Abstract

**Background.** Multicenter randomised clinical trials
recruit patients across multiple sites, introducing site as a
potential source of outcome variability. Whether and how site
should enter the analysis model — as a fixed effect, a random
effect, or as the basis for treatment-by-site interaction
testing — is a decision with consequences for power, type I
error, and the inferential target of the trial. This choice for
cross-sectional outcomes is already well studied
[@Kahan2013continuous; @Kahan2014binary]; less is known about
whether the same conclusions hold once outcomes are
longitudinal, with a subject-level random intercept layered
under the site structure. Regulatory guidance from ICH E9, the
FDA, and the EMA recommend that stratification variables be
included in the analysis model, but the choice between fixed
and random effects, and the inclusion or exclusion of
treatment-by-site interaction terms, has remained pragmatic.

**Methods.** We conduct a Monte Carlo simulation comparing
four linear-mixed analysis models (no site, site as fixed
effect, site as random effect, site-by-treatment interaction)
for a longitudinal, repeated-measures outcome, across six
scenarios: four crossing equal-versus-unequal, moderate site
sizes ($n \approx 20$ per site) with the presence-versus-absence
of true treatment-by-site interaction, one null-effect scenario
to assess empirical type I error, and one sparse-site scenario
(4-8 patients per site) targeting the regime in which the
cross-sectional literature reports the largest fixed-versus-random
advantage. The four primary scenarios are evaluated at
$n_{\text{sim}} = 1{,}000$ replicates; the null and sparse-site
scenarios use a reduced-replicate confirmatory run
($n_{\text{sim}} = 300$; see the Discussion and the Scenario 5-6
source chunks for the full-scale command). Bias, empirical SE,
model-based SE, power or type I error, coverage, and a
converged/singular/nonconverged/error convergence classification
are reported, each with its Monte Carlo SE.

**Results.** Adjusting for site, by any of the three methods
examined, outperforms omitting it whenever site contributes true
outcome variability, consistent with @Localio2001adjustments and
@Kahan2013continuous. Within this simulation, however, the
fixed- and random-effects models are not distinguishable from
each other once Monte Carlo error is taken into account, in
either the moderate or sparse-site regimes examined; we do not
reproduce, for this longitudinal setting, the fixed-versus-random
precision advantage reported by @Kahan2013continuous and
@edgarIncludingRandomCentre2021 for cross-sectional outcomes.
When no true treatment-by-site interaction exists, including the
interaction term expends degrees of freedom without benefit and
reduces power. Empirical type I error for the site-adjusted
models is in the vicinity of the nominal 0.05 level in the
reduced-replicate null scenario.

**Conclusions.** Site should be included in the analysis model,
as either a fixed or random effect, when site is a
stratification variable or contributes to outcome variability;
this simulation does not provide evidence, in the longitudinal
setting studied here, that the choice between fixed and random
effects for site materially affects precision, power, or
coverage. The treatment-by-site interaction term should be
included only when there is a strong a priori reason to expect
treatment effect heterogeneity across sites. The simulation
evidence supports the regulatory recommendation that
stratification variables enter the analysis as covariates, but
does not by itself resolve the fixed-versus-random choice for
longitudinal outcomes; see Discussion for scope limitations of
the reduced-replicate scenarios.

# Introduction

We address a key question in the analysis of data from multi-site
randomized clinical trials: whether and how to include site (or
centre) as a covariate in the analysis model. The question is
not merely academic. The choice of whether to adjust for site,
and whether to treat it as a fixed or random effect, can
influence estimates of treatment effect, standard errors,
confidence interval width, and statistical power
[@Localio2001adjustments; @Kahan2013continuous].

Multicenter trials are conducted to increase enrollment rates
and improve the generalizability of findings across clinical
settings. However, the inclusion of multiple sites introduces a
source of variability that complicates the analysis. Patients
within a site tend to be more similar to one another than to
patients at other sites, owing to shared clinical practices,
patient populations, and local standards of care. This
within-site correlation, or clustering, violates the independence
assumption underlying many standard statistical methods
[@Localio2001adjustments].

## Regulatory context

Both international and national regulatory bodies have addressed
the role of covariates, including site, in the analysis of
clinical trials. The ICH E9 guideline states that 'factors on
which randomisation has been stratified should be accounted for
later in the analysis' [@ICHE9guideline]. When randomization is
stratified by site, this implies that site should appear in the
analysis model. The United States Food and Drug Administration
(FDA) 2023 guidance on covariate adjustment reinforces this
position, recommending that stratification variables be included
in the primary analysis model [@FDA2023covariate]. The European
Medicines Agency (EMA) similarly advises that stratification
factors be incorporated unless stratification was performed for
purely administrative reasons [@EMA2015covariate].

## The case for adjusting for site

The primary statistical argument for including site in the
analysis model is that it can reduce residual variance, thereby
increasing the precision of treatment effect estimates and
improving power [@Kahan2014rewards]. When outcome rates or levels
differ substantially across sites, whether because of differences
in patient populations, diagnostic practices, or supportive care,
failing to account for this heterogeneity leaves variance
unexplained in the error term. Adjustment for site absorbs this
between-site variability and can yield narrower confidence
intervals for the treatment effect [@Kahan2013continuous;
@edgarIncludingRandomCentre2021].

A further argument concerns the validity of inference when
randomization has been stratified by site. @kahanImproperAnalysisTrials2012
demonstrated that stratified randomization induces correlation
between treatment groups within strata. If the analysis ignores
this structure, standard errors are biased upward, confidence
intervals are too wide, and power is reduced.
@linschotenIncorrectlyAnalysingStratified2022 provided a
clinical example in which failure to adjust for stratification
factors led to a false negative conclusion.

Site adjustment is a special case of the broader,
well-established literature on covariate adjustment for
precision in randomized trials, but is distinct from it in one
respect relevant to design: site is typically a stratification
factor set by the allocation scheme itself
[@Pocock1975allocation], rather than a prognostic baseline
covariate chosen for its association with outcome. The general
case for adjusting for prognostic baseline covariates,
including via ANCOVA, is made on model-robust grounds by
@wangAnalysisCovarianceRandomized2019 and treated at length in
the classical trials-design literature [@Fleiss1986design];
@wangUtilitiesPitfallsStratified2022 review the utilities and
pitfalls of stratified analysis more generally. This paper
addresses the narrower, site-specific question of how (fixed,
random, or interaction) rather than the more general question of
whether to adjust for a prognostic baseline covariate, which is
outside its scope.

## Fixed versus random effects

A central debate concerns whether site should enter the model as
a fixed or random effect. Fixed effects treat each site as a
separate parameter to be estimated, making no assumptions about
the distribution of site effects but consuming degrees of freedom
proportional to the number of sites. Random effects assume site
effects are drawn from a normal distribution, estimating only the
variance of that distribution and thereby requiring fewer
parameters [@Falissard1996center].

@Kahan2013continuous conducted a simulation study comparing fixed
and random centre effects for continuous outcomes across 378
scenarios. Random effects performed as well as or better than
fixed effects in all scenarios, with notable advantages when the
number of patients per site was small (10 or fewer) or when there
was imbalance between treatment arms within sites.
@Kahan2014binary extended these findings to binary outcomes,
comparing fixed effects, random effects, generalized estimating
equations (GEEs), and Mantel-Haenszel methods.

The practical relevance of this comparison is underscored by
@Kahan2015fewevents, who reviewed 206 multicenter trials in four
major medical journals and found that the median number of events
per centre-treatment arm combination was just 3, with 50% of
trials having fewer than 3 events per centre-treatment
combination. Fixed-effects models require substantial data per
site to perform well; in the majority of real trials, this
condition is not met [@kimAnalysisMulticenterClinical2020].

## Treatment-by-site interaction

If site effects on outcome vary, a natural question is whether
the treatment effect itself varies across sites, that is, whether
a treatment-by-site interaction exists. A qualitative interaction,
where the direction of the treatment effect reverses at some
sites, has major clinical implications: it suggests that the
treatment may be harmful for some patient populations
[@GailSimon1985qualitative]. However, tests for treatment-by-site
interaction are typically underpowered because individual sites
rarely enroll enough patients to estimate site-specific treatment
effects precisely [@edgarIncludingRandomCentre2021].

@Agresti2000strategies discussed strategies for handling
treatment-by-centre interaction with binary outcomes, noting that
random effects models smooth extreme site-specific estimates and
provide more stable inference than fixed effects when some sites
contribute sparse data. @Islam2024centerlevel reviewed recent
practice and confirmed that the choice of method for handling
centre effects can materially affect trial conclusions.

## Heterogeneous site sizes

Real multicenter trials rarely have equal enrollment across
sites. Some sites may contribute hundreds of patients while
others contribute fewer than ten. This heterogeneity in site
size interacts with the choice of analytic method.
Fixed-effects models can lead to patient exclusion when sites
have observations in only one treatment arm (a common occurrence
with small sites), whereas random-effects models borrow strength
across sites and avoid this problem
[@Kahan2015fewevents; @kimAnalysisMulticenterClinical2020].
@Localio2001adjustments provided an overview of the analytic
challenges introduced by clustering, confounding, and effect
modification in multicenter studies, emphasizing that the
correlation of outcomes within sites must be addressed to obtain
valid inference.

## Present study

Despite the extensive methodological literature, uncertainty
persists about when and how to adjust for site in practice.
The existing simulation studies have focused primarily on
cross-sectional outcomes. In many clinical trials, however,
outcomes are measured longitudinally over multiple visits,
introducing an additional layer of within-subject correlation that
interacts with the between-site structure. We use Monte Carlo
simulation to compare four analysis strategies for a longitudinal
outcome in a multicenter trial: (1) ignoring site
entirely, (2) including site as a fixed effect, (3) including
site as a random effect, and (4) including a site-by-treatment
interaction term. We evaluate these strategies under equal and
unequal, moderate site sizes, with and without true
treatment-by-site interaction; under a null treatment effect, to
assess empirical type I error; and under a sparse-site regime
(4-8 patients per site), the condition under which the
cross-sectional literature reports the clearest fixed-versus-random
advantage. We assess bias, power or type I error, coverage, and a
converged/singular/nonconverged/error convergence classification.

# Methods

## ADEMP structure

Following Morris, White, and Crowther [-@morris2019using], the
simulation is reported under the ADEMP framework.

- **Aims.** Compare four strategies for incorporating site information
  in multicenter trial analyses (no site adjustment, fixed site
  effects, random site effects, treatment-by-site interaction) across
  scenarios crossing balanced vs imbalanced site sizes with and
  without true treatment-by-site heterogeneity.
- **Data-generating mechanism.** Detailed in the next subsection.
- **Estimand.** The overall treatment effect $\delta$; when
  treatment-by-site variance is non-zero, the site-size-weighted
  average of site-specific effects.
- **Methods.** Four linear mixed models implemented via
  \texttt{lme4::lmer} differing only in how site is entered.
- **Performance measures.** Convergence rate, bias, empirical SE,
  MSE, mean model-based SE, power at $\alpha = 0.05$, and coverage
  of 95\% CIs, each reported with its Monte Carlo SE per Morris
  Table 6.

## Data generating model

We simulate data from a two-arm parallel-group multicenter trial
with a continuous longitudinal outcome measured at $T = 4$
equally spaced time points. The model for the outcome $Y_{ijk}$
of subject $j$ at site $i$ and time $k$ is:

$$
Y_{ijk} = \alpha_i + (\beta + \gamma_i) \cdot \text{Trt}_{ij}
  + \delta \cdot t_k + u_j + \epsilon_{ijk}
$$

where $\alpha_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_s)$ is the random site
intercept, $\beta$ is the true treatment effect,
$\gamma_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{s \times t})$ is the random
treatment-by-site interaction, $\delta = 0.05$ is a linear time
slope, $u_j \sim N(0, 0.25)$ is a subject-level random
intercept, and $\epsilon_{ijk} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_e)$ is
residual error.

## Simulation scenarios

We examine four primary scenarios defined by crossing two
factors:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Site size}: equal (20 patients per site) versus
    unequal (exponentially distributed with mean 20,
    minimum 4)
  \item \textbf{Treatment-by-site interaction}: absent
    ($\sigma^2_{s \times t} = 0$) versus present
    ($\sigma^2_{s \times t} = 0.15$)
\end{itemize}

In all four primary scenarios, we set $K = 20$ sites,
$\beta = 0.30$, $\sigma^2_s = 0.25$, and $\sigma^2_e = 1.0$.
Within each site, subjects are randomized 1:1 to treatment and
control. For the unequal-size condition, the vector of per-site
sample sizes is drawn once per scenario call and reused across
all $n_{\mathrm{sim}}$ replications of that scenario, rather than
resampled at every replication; "unequal site sizes" therefore
describes one fixed, arbitrary site-size allocation, analogous to
treating total sample size as a fixed design factor, not a
distribution over designs that varies by replicate.

Two additional scenarios probe conditions the primary four do not
test (Results, Scenarios 5-6): a null-effect scenario
($\beta = 0$, equal site sizes, no interaction) to assess
empirical type I error, and a sparse-site scenario (4-8 patients
per site, drawn once per scenario as above) to test the regime in
which the cross-sectional fixed-versus-random literature reports
the clearest advantage for random effects
[@Kahan2013continuous; @Kahan2015fewevents].

## Analysis models

For each simulated dataset, we fit four linear mixed models
using the \texttt{lme4} package [@R-lme4]:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{No site}: \texttt{y \~{} trt + time + (1|subj)}
  \item \textbf{Site fixed}:
    \texttt{y \~{} trt + time + site + (1|subj)}
  \item \textbf{Site random}:
    \texttt{y \~{} trt + time + (1|site) + (1|subj)}
  \item \textbf{Site $\times$ treatment}:
    \texttt{y \~{} trt*site + time + (1|subj)}
\end{enumerate}

## Performance metrics

For each model across 1,000 replications, we compute:

- **Bias**: mean estimated treatment effect minus true value
  ($\beta = 0.30$)
- **Empirical SE**: standard deviation of estimates across
  replications
- **Mean model SE**: average of model-based standard errors
- **Power** (or, in the null-effect scenario, **type I error**):
  proportion of replications with $p < 0.05$
- **Coverage**: proportion of nominal 95\% confidence intervals
  containing the true value
- **Convergence rate**: proportion of replications classified as
  fully converged, out of four mutually exclusive outcome
  categories per fit (converged, singular, nonconverged, error).
  `lme4` signals optimizer failure-to-converge and singular-fit
  conditions as warnings rather than errors, so this
  classification captures `lme4` warnings via
  `withCallingHandlers()` and checks `lme4::isSingular()` and
  `fit@optinfo$conv$opt`, rather than only catching R errors.

```{r sim-seed, cache=FALSE}
# Morris, White, and Crowther (2019) §4.1: pin RNGkind and set the
# seed ONCE at the start of the program. `sim_site_covariate()` no
# longer accepts a `seed` argument; each scenario consumes state from
# this single stream in sequence. Differences between scenarios then
# reflect DGM differences, not distinct RNG starting points.
#
# `sim_seed` is stored in a variable (rather than hand-typed only
# inside `set.seed()`) so the Reproducibility section below can quote
# it via inline R and cannot drift out of sync with the code, per
# whitepaper issue 2.2.
sim_seed <- 20260312
RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")
set.seed(sim_seed)
```

For coverage MCSE $\leq 0.7$ pp at 0.95, $n_{\mathrm{sim}} \geq 970$;
$n_{\mathrm{sim}} = 1000$ gives coverage MCSE $\approx 0.69$ pp.

```{r run-sim-equal-nointeract, cache=TRUE}
res_eq_no <- sim_site_covariate(
  n_sim = 1000, n_sites = 20,
  site_size = "equal", true_trt = 0.30,
  site_sd = 0.50, trt_site_sd = 0.0
)
```

```{r run-sim-unequal-nointeract, cache=TRUE}
res_uneq_no <- sim_site_covariate(
  n_sim = 1000, n_sites = 20,
  site_size = "unequal", true_trt = 0.30,
  site_sd = 0.50, trt_site_sd = 0.0
)
```

```{r run-sim-equal-interact, cache=TRUE}

  n_sim = 1000, n_sites = 20,
  site_size = "equal", true_trt = 0.30,

)
```

```{r run-sim-unequal-interact, cache=TRUE}

```

# Results

## Headline findings

```{r headline-11, include=FALSE}
summ_eq_no   <- summarise_sim(res_eq_no,   true_trt = 0.30)
summ_uneq_no <- summarise_sim(res_uneq_no, true_trt = 0.30)
summ_eq_int  <- summarise_sim(res_eq_int,  true_trt = 0.30)
summ_uneq_int<- summarise_sim(res_uneq_int,true_trt = 0.30)
all_summ <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(summ_eq_no, scenario = "Equal, no interaction"),
  dplyr::mutate(summ_uneq_no, scenario = "Unequal, no interaction"),
  dplyr::mutate(summ_eq_int, scenario = "Equal, with interaction"),
  dplyr::mutate(summ_uneq_int, scenario = "Unequal, with interaction")
)
bias_max <- all_summ |>
  dplyr::slice_max(abs(bias), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
cov_range <- range(all_summ$coverage, na.rm = TRUE)
pow_by_model <- all_summ |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(pow_mean = mean(power, na.rm = TRUE))
```

We find that across four scenarios crossing balanced vs
imbalanced site sizes with and without true
treatment-by-site heterogeneity, all four analysis models
produced absolute bias below
`r sprintf('%.3f', abs(bias_max$bias))` (worst case:
`r bias_max$model` under "`r bias_max$scenario`", MCSE
`r sprintf('%.3f', bias_max$mcse_bias)`). Coverage of 95\%
confidence intervals across all combinations fell in
[`r sprintf('%.3f', cov_range[1])`,
`r sprintf('%.3f', cov_range[2])`]. Mean power by model
(averaged across scenarios) was:
`r paste(sprintf('%s = %.2f', pow_by_model$model,
pow_by_model$pow_mean), collapse = ', ')`. All performance
measures are reported with their Morris Table 6
Monte Carlo SEs in the per-scenario tables below.

## Scenario 1: Equal site sizes, no interaction

```{r tab-equal-no}
tab1 <- summarise_sim(res_eq_no, true_trt = 0.30)
tab1 |>
  mutate(
    Bias = fmt_mcse(bias, mcse_bias),
    Power = fmt_mcse(power, mcse_power),
    Coverage = fmt_mcse(coverage, mcse_coverage),
    model = dplyr::recode(model, !!!model_labels)
  ) |>
  select(model, Bias, empirical_se, mean_model_se,
         Power, Coverage, convergence_rate, n_fit) |>
  kable(
    format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE,
    caption = paste(
      "Performance of four analysis models: equal",
      "site sizes, no treatment-by-site interaction.",
      "Bias, Power, and Coverage are shown as",
      "estimate (Monte Carlo SE)."
    ),
    digits = 3, escape = FALSE,
    col.names = c(
      "Model", "Bias (MCSE)", "Emp. SE",
      "Model SE", "Power (MCSE)", "Coverage (MCSE)",
      "Conv.", "N fit"
    )
  ) |>
  kable_styling(
    latex_options = c("hold_position"),
    font_size = 8
  )
```

## Scenario 5: Null treatment effect (Type I error)

The Abstract states that the choice of analysis model has
"consequences for power, type I error." Scenarios 1-4 all set
$\beta = 0.30$, so the reported "power" columns above are
true-positive rates; no scenario tests the null. This
section adds a null-effect scenario ($\beta = 0$, equal site
sizes, no treatment-by-site interaction, $\sigma^2_s = 0.50$)
so that empirical Type I error can be reported directly
(whitepaper issue 2.1).

```{r run-sim-null, cache=TRUE}
# TODO(remediation): this scenario was run at a reduced replicate

```{r tab-null}

tab_null |>
  mutate(
    `Type I error` = fmt_mcse(power, mcse_power),
    model = dplyr::recode(model, !!!model_labels)
  ) |>
  select(model, `Type I error`, coverage, convergence_rate,

  kable(

At `r n_sim_null` replications, empirical Type I error is close
to, but for the site-adjusted models nominally somewhat below,
the target 0.05 (Table 5); the "No site" model's Type I error is
below the site-adjusted models', consistent with the
site-adjusted models targeting a narrower error stratum once site
variance is absorbed rather than left in the residual. Because
this run uses a reduced replicate count, the reported MCSEs are
correspondingly wider than in Scenarios 1-4; the full
$n_{\mathrm{sim}} = 1000$ run noted in the TODO above should be
substituted before this becomes a headline claim.

## Scenario 6: Sparse site sizes

The Introduction motivates the fixed-versus-random comparison by
citing evidence that random effects show their clearest advantage
when sites contribute few patients (@Kahan2015fewevents: a
median of 3 events per centre-treatment arm across 206 published
trials). Scenarios 1-4 use $n \approx 20$ patients per site,
which does not test this regime (whitepaper issue 2.5). This
section adds a sparse-site scenario with 4-8 patients per site.

```{r run-sim-sparse, cache=TRUE}

#   res_sparse <- sim_site_covariate(
#     n_sim = 1000, n_sites = 20, site_size = "sparse",
#     true_trt = 0.30, site_sd = 0.50, trt_site_sd = 0.0
#   )
# then re-render with `bash tools/render.sh
# analysis/report/report.Rmd`.
sparse_rds <- "../data/derived_data/sim_sparse_n300.rds"
res_sparse <- readRDS(sparse_rds)
n_sim_sparse <- length(unique(res_sparse$sim))
```

```{r tab-sparse}
tab_sparse <- summarise_sim(res_sparse, true_trt = 0.30)
tab_sparse |>
  mutate(
    Bias = fmt_mcse(bias, mcse_bias),
    Power = fmt_mcse(power, mcse_power),
    Coverage = fmt_mcse(coverage, mcse_coverage),
    model = dplyr::recode(model, !!!model_labels)
  ) |>

         Power, Coverage, convergence_rate, n_fit) |>
  kable(
    format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE,
    caption = paste(
      "Performance of four analysis models: sparse site sizes",
      "(4-8 patients per site), reduced-replicate confirmatory",
      "run ($n_{\\mathrm{sim}} = 300$; see TODO in the source",
      "chunk for the full $n_{\\mathrm{sim}} = 1000$ command).",
      "Bias, Power, and Coverage are shown as estimate",
      "(Monte Carlo SE)."
    ),
    digits = 3, escape = FALSE,
    col.names = c(
      "Model", "Bias (MCSE)", "Emp. SE",
      "Model SE", "Power (MCSE)", "Coverage (MCSE)",

```

At `r n_sim_sparse` replications, the largest effect in Table 6
is between "No site" and the three site-adjusted models (power
`r sprintf('%.3f', tab_sparse$power[tab_sparse$model == "no_site"])`
versus approximately
`r sprintf('%.3f', mean(tab_sparse$power[tab_sparse$model != "no_site"]))`),
not between the fixed- and random-effects models specifically,
whose power estimates
(`r sprintf('%.3f', tab_sparse$power[tab_sparse$model == "site_fixed"])`
vs
`r sprintf('%.3f', tab_sparse$power[tab_sparse$model == "site_random"])`)
differ by less than one Monte Carlo SE. Even in this sparse-site
regime, this simulation does not reproduce a fixed-versus-random
advantage of the kind reported by @Kahan2013continuous for
cross-sectional outcomes; see the Discussion for interpretation.

## Comparison of bias and power across scenarios

```{r fig-bias, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3.5, fig.cap="Bias of the treatment effect estimate across four models and four simulation scenarios."}
all_results <- bind_rows(
  res_eq_no |> mutate(
    scenario = "Equal, no interaction"),
  res_uneq_no |> mutate(
    scenario = "Unequal, no interaction"),
  res_eq_int |> mutate(
    scenario = "Equal, with interaction"),
  res_uneq_int |> mutate(
    scenario = "Unequal, with interaction")
)

all_results |>
  filter(converged) |>
  mutate(
    model = factor(
      model,
      levels = c("no_site", "site_fixed",
                  "site_random", "site_x_trt"),
      labels = c("No site", "Fixed",
                 "Random", "Site x Trt")
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = estimate - 0.30)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey50"
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "grey85", outlier.size = 0.5
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~scenario, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Analysis model",
    y = "Bias (estimate - 0.30)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 7
    )
  )
```

```{r fig-power, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3.5, fig.cap="Power to detect the treatment effect across four models and four simulation scenarios."}
power_dat <- all_results |>
  filter(converged) |>
  mutate(
    model = factor(
      model,
      levels = c("no_site", "site_fixed",
                  "site_random", "site_x_trt"),

                 "Random", "Site x Trt")
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(model, scenario) |>

    power = mean(pvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),

power_dat |>
  ggplot(aes(

  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 7),
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45, hjust = 1
    )
  )
```

```{r fig-coverage, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3.5, fig.cap="Coverage of nominal 95 percent confidence intervals across four models and four simulation scenarios. The dashed line indicates the nominal 95 percent level."}

  filter(converged) |>

# Discussion

The simulation results illuminate several practical
considerations for the inclusion of site in the analysis of
multicenter trials with longitudinal outcomes, which we shall
now take up in turn.

First, in the moderate, near-balanced site sizes used in
Scenarios 1-4 ($n \approx 20$ patients per site), the fixed- and
random-effects models are numerically almost indistinguishable:
Tables 1-4 show the same model-based SE, power, and coverage for
`site_fixed` and `site_random` to the displayed precision, and
the Monte Carlo SEs reported alongside each estimate confirm that
no cross-model gap in this simulation clears two MCSEs. This is
the expected behaviour under near-orthogonal allocation: because
treatment is assigned close to 1:1 within every site, the site
design matrix is close to orthogonal to treatment, so the
site-adjustment method has little effect on the treatment point
estimate or its precision at this site size. We therefore do
**not** find, in this simulation, a fixed-versus-random
precision advantage of the kind reported by @Kahan2013continuous
and @edgarIncludingRandomCentre2021 for the cross-sectional case;
Scenario 6 (sparse sites, 4-8 patients per site, the regime
those studies identify as the one in which the advantage should
be clearest) likewise shows no distinguishable fixed-versus-random
gap in this longitudinal setting, although this scenario was run
at a reduced replicate count (see TODO in the Scenario 6 source
chunk) and should be confirmed at $n_{\mathrm{sim}} = 1000$ before
being treated as a settled null result. What the simulation does
show consistently, across every scenario, is the much larger and
well-supported effect of adjusting for site at all versus omitting
it (see the "No site" versus site-adjusted comparison below), a
result already well established by @Localio2001adjustments and
@Kahan2013continuous rather than a novel finding of this study.

Second, when no true treatment-by-site interaction exists,
including an interaction term in the model expends degrees of
freedom without benefit, leading to reduced power relative to
simpler models. This finding supports the common recommendation
to include the interaction term only when there is a strong
a priori reason to expect treatment effect heterogeneity
across sites [@GailSimon1985qualitative;
@Agresti2000strategies].

Third, the regulatory guidance from ICH E9, the FDA, and the
EMA all converge on the recommendation that stratification
variables should be included in the analysis model
[@ICHE9guideline; @FDA2023covariate; @EMA2015covariate]. Our
simulation results support this recommendation: ignoring site
when it is a true source of outcome variability leads to
inflated residual variance and reduced power compared with
models that account for site.

Fourth, the "unequal" site-size condition in Scenarios 2 and 4
uses one arbitrary site-size allocation, drawn once per scenario
and reused across all replications of that scenario (a fixed
design factor, analogous to a fixed total sample size), rather
than a distribution over designs resampled at each replication;
this is a defensible ADEMP choice but is stated explicitly here
so that "unequal site sizes" is not read as implying sizes vary
by replicate.

Fifth, Scenario 5 (Table 5) reports empirical Type I error under
a null treatment effect, addressing the Abstract's reference to
"consequences for ... type I error," which no scenario tested in
the original design. At the reduced replicate count used for
this confirmatory run ($n_{\mathrm{sim}} = 300$; see the TODO in
the Scenario 5 source chunk for the full-scale command), Type I
error for the site-adjusted models is in the vicinity of the
nominal 0.05 level; the full $n_{\mathrm{sim}} = 1000$ run should
be substituted before this is treated as a precise estimate.

Several limitations warrant acknowledgment. The simulation
uses a relatively simple data-generating mechanism with
normally distributed outcomes, random intercepts only, and no
dropout or missing data. Real trials involve more complex
covariance structures, non-normal outcomes, and informative
missingness. Scenarios 5 and 6 were run at a reduced replicate
count under a separately seeded RNG stream rather than the single
pinned stream used for Scenarios 1-4 (see the Reproducibility
section); the exact commands to fold them into the main
$n_{\mathrm{sim}} = 1000$ sequence are noted as TODOs in their
respective source chunks. The results should be interpreted as
illustrating general principles rather than providing definitive
guidance for any specific trial design.

# Future research

Several directions merit further investigation:

1. **Non-normal outcomes.** Extending the simulation to binary
   and time-to-event endpoints would complement the present
   results for continuous outcomes and address the findings
   of @Kahan2014binary and
   @kimAnalysisMulticenterClinical2020 regarding sparse
   events per site.

2. **Complex covariance structures.** The present simulation
   uses compound symmetry (random intercept only) for both
   site and subject effects. Examining unstructured or
   autoregressive within-subject correlations, and allowing
   random slopes at the site level, would better approximate
   real longitudinal trial data.

3. **Informative site sizes.** When site size is correlated
   with patient characteristics or treatment effect, ignoring
   this informativeness may bias results. Methods that model
   the relationship between site size and outcome deserve
   attention.

4. **Adaptive designs.** In platform trials and other adaptive
   designs, sites may be added or dropped during the trial.
   The implications for site-effect adjustment in these
   settings are not well understood.

5. **Software tools.** Development of R functions or Shiny
   applications that allow trialists to explore the impact of
   different site-adjustment strategies on their specific
   trial design could facilitate informed pre-specification
   of analysis plans.

6. **Bayesian approaches.** Bayesian hierarchical models offer
   a natural framework for modelling site effects and
   treatment-by-site heterogeneity, with the additional
   advantage of incorporating prior information. Comparing
   frequentist and Bayesian approaches in the multicenter
   trial context would be valuable.

7. **Empirical review.** A systematic review of how site
   effects are handled in recently published trials in major
   medical journals (NEJM, JAMA, Lancet) would quantify
   current practice and identify gaps between methodological
   recommendations and applied work, extending the review by
   @Kahan2015fewevents.

# Data availability statement

The R simulation engine, driver scripts, and cached results
that populate the manuscript's tables and figures are openly
available in the `sitecovariate` project repository.
Specific paths are listed in the Reproducibility section
below.

# Reproducibility

```{r reproducibility-info, include=FALSE}
r_version_string <- R.version.string
sim_pkgs <- c("lme4", "dplyr")
report_pkgs <- c("kableExtra", "ggplot2", "knitr", "rmarkdown",
                  "bookdown")
sim_pkg_versions <- vapply(
  sim_pkgs,
  function(p) as.character(utils::packageVersion(p)),
  character(1)
)
sim_pkg_str <- paste(
  sprintf("`%s` (%s)", sim_pkgs, sim_pkg_versions), collapse = ", "
)
```

This section is generated from `sessionInfo()` and the `sim_seed`
variable set in the `sim-seed` chunk above, rather than hand-typed,
so it cannot drift out of sync with the code (whitepaper issue 2.2).

This manuscript was rendered with `r r_version_string`. The
simulation pipeline (`analysis/scripts/sim_site_covariate.R`) is a
plain serial `for` loop over replications, using base R's `rnorm()`
for all data generation and `r sim_pkg_str` for model fitting and
summarisation; it does not call `MASS::mvrnorm()` and there is no
parallel backend (no `furrr` or `future` usage anywhere in the
repository). Report generation and tables additionally use
`r paste(sprintf("\`%s\`", report_pkgs), collapse = ", ")`, plus
`rmarkdown`/`bookdown` for the manuscript build. The project's
`renv.lock` and `Dockerfile` pin R 4.6.0 for the containerized build
(`rocker/verse:4.6.0`); the R version actually used for this
particular render is reported above and may differ from the pinned
container version when rendered on the host outside Docker.

**Random-number generator.** The simulation driver follows
@morris2019using §4.1: `RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")` is pinned and
`set.seed(sim_seed)` is called once, at the single `sim-seed` chunk
above, before any scenario runs (`sim_seed` = `r sim_seed`).
`sim_site_covariate()` does not accept a `seed` argument and does
not call `set.seed()` internally; all four scenarios consume state
from this one RNG stream in sequence, so differences between
scenarios reflect the data-generating mechanism, not distinct RNG
starting points. Per-replicate `.Random.seed` snapshots are stored
as an attribute of each scenario's return value for diagnostic
reproducibility of any individual replication.

**Data and code availability.** The simulation engine is at
`analysis/scripts/sim_site_covariate.R`. Cached simulation
outputs are at `analysis/data/`. The manuscript source,
bibliography (`references.bib`), and CSL file are at
`analysis/report/`.

# ADEMP compliance statement

We audited this simulation study against the reporting
standards proposed by Morris, White, and Crowther
[-@morris2019using]. This section was previously nested under
the "References" heading, where it did not belong (whitepaper
issue 3.3); it is now its own top-level section. The audit was
re-run against the current code as part of remediating
`docs/pub_review_whitepaper_2026-08-16.md`; the corrected
scorecard and verdict are recorded at
`docs/morris-audit-2026-08-16.md`, which supersedes the original
`docs/morris-audit-2026-04-17.md` (left unmodified as a
historical record).

**Verdict:** Substantially compliant (previously "Partially
compliant").

**Gaps identified in the 2026-04-17 audit, now resolved:**

- The RNG seed is set exactly once, in the `sim-seed` chunk
  above, before any scenario runs; `sim_site_covariate()` does
  not call `set.seed()` internally.
- `summarise_sim()` computes a Monte Carlo SE for every reported
  metric, and Tables 1-6 now display these MCSEs directly
  (previously reported only in inline text).
- `n_sim = 1000` for the four primary scenarios is derived from a
  target coverage MCSE, stated explicitly in the Methods section.

**Gap identified in the 2026-08-16 referee review, now resolved:**

- Convergence was previously defined only as "did not raise an R
  error." `fit_lmer_safely()` in `sim_site_covariate.R` now
  classifies every model fit as converged, singular,
  nonconverged, or error, capturing `lme4` warnings via
  `withCallingHandlers()` and checking `lme4::isSingular()` and
  `fit@optinfo$conv$opt`.

**Remaining gap, disclosed rather than resolved:** Scenarios 5-6
(null-effect and sparse-site) were run at a reduced replicate
count under a separately seeded RNG stream, for time-budget
reasons; see the TODOs in their source chunks for the exact
commands to fold them into the main $n_{\mathrm{sim}} = 1000$
sequence.
